Why

Why California leads on every island

California is simply the biggest pool of people within about 2,400–2,700 miles of Hawaiʻi. Per resident, Californians buy at about the same rate as people in Washington, Nevada, Oregon and Utah (30–41 buyers per million in 2025), and five to six times the rate of Texas or Florida. Distance decides who is in range, and income decides who buys within it. That is why the Bay Area and Los Angeles lead.

  1. StrongSize and location: the most populous state within about 2,400–2,700 miles, buying per resident like Washington, Nevada, Oregon and Utah
  2. StrongThe Bay Area and LA are the two largest pools of nearby high-income households and the two biggest gateways
  3. ModerateVisitor familiarity: California sends about 38% of US visitors, and its share of buyers matches
  4. ModerateNonstop flights carry the demand more than they create it
  5. ModerateWealth: within flying range, income decides how many buy and how much they spend
  6. WeakFamily ties: California is Hawaiʻi's largest two-way migration partner
  7. WeakRemote work: a 2021–22 boost, not the reason for the ranking
  8. WeakTime zone: a minor convenience
  9. WeakTaxes are not a driver: from 2027 Hawaiʻi taxes high earners about as heavily as California does
Reading the data

On the neighbor islands most California dollars go to the top of the market, but not all purchases: on Hawaiʻi Island in 2025, 112 of California's 406 purchases were Puna properties averaging about $230K. In 2025, California buyers on the neighbor islands paid on average 2 to 3.6 times what local buyers paid (Maui County 2.0×, Kauaʻi 2.8×, Hawaiʻi Island 3.6×). On Oʻahu they paid close to local prices (about $1.03M against $0.87M), which fits relocation, family and military moves, though that mix cannot be measured. California buyers fell 14% in January–June 2026 while Washington buyers rose 17%.

For local families

California supplied about 38% of mainland buyers in 2008–15 and 37–46% in 2024–26, so that demand will not vanish with a tax change or a rate cycle. On Oʻahu, Californians made about 6% of 2025 purchases. Rules aimed at homes that are not a main residence, such as vacation-rental limits and Honolulu's Residential A tax tiers, reach these buyers far more than income-tax changes do.

The full explanation, each driver as checked, and 28 sources

The checked answer

California is the top out-of-state buyer state on every island in 2024, 2025 and January-June 2026 (Title Guaranty). The main reason is that it is by far the biggest pool of people living within about 2,400-2,700 miles of Hawaii, not that Californians are unusually eager buyers. In 2025 Title Guaranty counted 1,271 California buyers: 38% of the 3,314 out-of-state US buyers and 4.6 times runner-up Washington. Per million residents, California (32) bought at about the same rate as Washington (35), Nevada (41), Oregon (31) and Utah (30), and 5-6 times the rate of Texas (5.5) or Florida (6.8). The same pattern held in 2024. California's roughly 38% share matches its share of US visitors (38-41% in every normal year since 2013) and its 38.6% share of mainland purchases in 2008-15. Distance decides who is in range; income decides who buys within it. Florida and Texas have about as many $1M-plus tax filers per tax return as Washington or Nevada, yet buy at a fifth of the rate. Inside California, Oahu homes owned per resident run from about 466 per million in the Bay Area and 240 in Los Angeles-Orange County down to 44 in the Inland Empire, which has the same flight time and its own nonstop service. That is why the Bay Area and LA dominate: they are the two largest concentrations of nearby high-income households and the two largest air gateways. They are roughly tied in absolute ownership, but per resident the Bay Area owns about twice as much, in line with its higher income per tax return. Nonstop seats (57.5% of July 2026 domestic seats from California) and repeat visiting (82% of West Coast visitors are repeat visitors) are the channels this demand flows through rather than independent causes, since airlines put seats where demand already is. Family and military links add a steady base, especially on Oahu, where California buyers pay close to local prices. California is Hawaii's largest two-way migration partner, and San Diego County is the top county source of households moving to Oahu. These links cannot be measured separately. Taxes do not explain the pattern: from 2027 Hawaii taxes most high earners at the same or higher marginal rates as California, and most California buyers keep California residency. Remote work raised volumes in 2021-22, but California led long before. The lead is narrowing: California buyers fell 14% in January-June 2026 while Washington buyers rose 17%. California visitor arrivals are 12% below their 2022 peak, though still 6% above 2019. Confidence is high on the pattern and medium on how much each mechanism contributes. Title Guaranty classifies buyers by address, publishes only its top 10 states and has no metro detail, so the metro comparisons rely on owner rolls of existing homes.

Each driver, as checked

  • Size and location: the most populous state within about 2,400–2,700 miles, buying per resident like Washington, Nevada, Oregon and Utah (strong; supported by the check). California ranks #1 mainly because it is by far the most populous state within about 2,400-2,700 miles of Hawaii. Per resident it buys at about the same rate as Washington, Nevada, Oregon and Utah (30-41 per million in 2025, 26-44 in 2024) and 5-6 times the rate of Texas or Florida. Farther western states such as Arizona and Colorado buy at one-third to two-thirds of the California rate. There is no California-only premium in buyer counts.
  • The Bay Area and LA are the two largest pools of nearby high-income households and the two biggest gateways (strong; supported by the check). The Bay Area and LA-Orange County lead because they are the two largest pools of nearby high-income households and the two largest air gateways. In absolute terms they are about tied: depending on whether institutional addresses are counted, either can lead on Oahu, and they are near-equal on Maui. Per resident, the Bay Area visits and owns about twice as much as LA-OC, in line with roughly 1.5-2.4 times the income per tax return. Seattle shows the same pattern at a smaller scale.
  • Visitor familiarity: California sends about 38% of US visitors, and its share of buyers matches (moderate; weakened by the check). California sends about 38% of US visitors, and its buyer share matches that, so the visitor pipeline carries California demand. But visiting does not explain buying on its own. Conversion to ownership varies about fourfold within California by income, Florida converts at twice California's rate, and owners' own trips inflate the repeat-visitor counts. Treat visitor volume as a channel and a correlate, not an independent cause.
  • Nonstop flights carry the demand more than they create it (moderate; weakened by the check). Dense nonstop service from California makes a Hawaii second home easy to use. But it mostly follows California demand rather than creating it, and island-level seat shares do not track island-level buyer shares. Treat air access as an enabler (moderate); distance is the part that is truly fixed.
  • Wealth: within flying range, income decides how many buy and how much they spend (moderate; weakened by the check). Wealth works together with distance. Across states, nearness decides who is in range: wealthy Florida and Texas buy little. Within reach, income strongly drives both how many buy and how much they spend. Inside California, Oahu ownership per resident is about ten times higher in the Bay Area than in the Inland Empire, and California buyers pay 2-3.6 times local prices on the neighbor islands. Since 2019, Bay Area home equity has lost ground to Hawaii prices; LA-OC equity has not.
  • Family ties: California is Hawaiʻi's largest two-way migration partner (weak; weakened by the check). California is Hawaii's largest two-way migration partner and home to a large community with Hawaiʻi roots, which adds a steady base of family, returning-resident and relocation buyers, mostly on Oahu. Per resident, though, California's diaspora is thinner than Nevada's, Washington's, Oregon's or Utah's. Ties help explain volume and those states' slightly higher rates, not California's #1 rank. The effect cannot be separated from distance.
  • Remote work: a 2021–22 boost, not the reason for the ranking (weak; weakened by the check). Remote work lifted mainland buying in 2021-22 (+80% statewide in 2021) and pulled richer Bay Area households to Hawaii (average AGI about $188-189K in 2020-22). Gross Bay Area inflows rose about a third to a half while moves the other way fell, and both had normalized by 2022-23. California led well before remote work existed, so remote work is not why it ranks first.
  • Time zone: a minor convenience (weak; supported by the check). A minor convenience for Pacific-time remote workers and part-year residents. It cannot be measured separately from distance.
  • Taxes are not a driver: from 2027 Hawaiʻi taxes high earners about as heavily as California does (weak; supported by the check). Taxes do not explain California's lead. Most California buyers keep California residency. From 2027, Hawaii will tax high earners at about the same or higher marginal rates than California across most of the $325K-$1M range. The one real difference, Hawaii's 7.25% cap on capital gains, matters only to a few relocating sellers of large gains.

Why

Why Washington, Oregon, Alaska, Colorado and Utah buy more per resident than Texas or Florida

The real pattern is the West against everyone else. By raw count in 2025, Texas (175) and Florida (159) outranked Colorado (136), Oregon (133) and Utah (105); in January–June 2026 Florida (41) fell behind all three. Per resident, though, Alaska, Nevada, Washington, Oregon, Utah and Colorado buy three to more than ten times as often as Texas or Florida. The western states are closer, have more nonstop flights and send far more visitors. Each island pattern has its own reason. Seattle flies nonstop to all four main airports. Alaskans fly Anchorage–Kona in winter and buy where prices are lowest. Colorado and Utah visitors favor Kauaʻi, but their purchases there are few and unstable.

  1. StrongFlight network: Seattle serves all four islands, and Anchorage–Kona flies in winter
  2. StrongLāʻie and BYU–Hawaiʻi ties explain where some Utah owners are
  3. ModerateVisitor funnel: western states send far more visitors per resident (a correlation, not proof)
  4. ModerateWinter escape: strong for Alaska only
  5. ModeratePrice: Hawaiʻi Island is cheapest, which shapes where Alaskans and Oregonians buy, not whether they buy
  6. ModerateFamily and migration ties: real for Nevada, Washington, Oregon and Alaska
  7. WeakColorado and Utah on Kauaʻi: clear in visitor data, small and unstable in buyer data
Reading the data

Per resident, in 2025 Nevada bought 41 Hawaiʻi homes per million residents, Washington 35, Oregon 31 and Utah 30, against about 6 for Texas and 7 for Florida. Within the West, visitor rates do not predict which state buys more. Colorado's 2025 Kauaʻi spike came largely from 12 Hanalei purchases averaging about $460K in one half-year, so it may not repeat.

For local families

On Hawaiʻi Island, buyers from Alaska, Oregon and Washington are mostly not luxury buyers, and some compete directly with local families for cheap Puna lots and starter homes. On Kauaʻi, Utah buyers are mostly in Poʻipū and Princeville and paid about $1.9M on average in 2025, well above local budgets; Colorado buyers averaged about $1.1M, close to the $1.0M local-buyer average.

The full explanation, each driver as checked, and 26 sources

The checked answer

The question's premise only partly holds. By raw purchase counts, Texas (175 in 2025) and Florida (159) outrank Colorado (136), Oregon (133) and Utah (105) statewide, Nevada (134) is level with them, and Alaska never appears in the statewide top 10 for a full year. What sets these five states apart is buying per resident and on particular islands. In 2025, Alaska bought at least 75 Hawaii homes per million residents, Nevada 41, Washington 35, California 32, Oregon 31, Utah 30 and Colorado 23, compared with about 6 for Texas and 7 for Florida. The clearest pattern is the West against everyone else. Western residents live closer, have more nonstop flights, visit Hawaii far more often (Washington 8.9, Oregon 7.5 and Utah 6.5 visitors per 100 residents, against 1.1 for Texas), and come back more (6 to 8 trips on average, against 4 to 4.5). Within the West, though, visit rates do not predict which state buys more, so 'visiting leads to buying' is a correlation, not proof, and some repeat visitors are probably people who already own here. Each island pattern has its own explanation, and they differ in strength. Washington appears everywhere because Seattle, Alaska Air Group's largest hub, flies nonstop to all four main airports (1.47 million seats in 2025). Alaskans favor Hawaii Island because of the winter Anchorage–Kona nonstops, because 63% of their trips fall in November–March, and because prices are lowest there (they averaged about $708k, the lowest of any listed state). That still means about 70% of their purchases, not nearly all. Oregon's Hawaii Island lean is real but modest. Oregonians buy both in Kona/Kohala and on cheap Puna lots, and Californians buy even more Puna lots. Puna buying is about price, not flights: Hilo had no mainland nonstop from January 2023 until August 2026. Colorado and Utah visitors really do favor Kauai, even without a nonstop from Salt Lake City. But the buyer numbers are tiny (3 to 24 a year), Colorado's 2025 jump came largely from 12 sub-$500k Hanalei purchases in one half-year, and both states were back to an average share in early 2026. Their concentration in Poipu and Princeville mostly reflects Kauai's rule that vacation rentals are allowed mainly in resort zones. Utah's distinctive tie is the community around BYU–Hawaiʻi in Lāʻie on Oʻahu, but it is small: 55 of 944 Lāʻie parcels. It explains where some Utah owners are, not Utah's statewide rank. Three ideas do not hold up as reasons these states buy. Home-equity gains fail because Florida, Arizona and Nevada gained as much as or more than Utah or Washington and rarely buy. No state income tax fails because Texas and Florida have none and also rarely buy. Winter escape fails outside Alaska, because warm-weather Arizona sends a larger share of its trips in November–March than Colorado does. Military moves explain much of the Texas, Florida and Virginia buying on Oahu, where 27% of 2025 home-purchase loans were VA loans. Confidence is medium for the West-against-the-rest pattern and for Washington and Alaska, and low for Colorado and Utah on Kauai.

Each driver, as checked

  • Flight network: Seattle serves all four islands, and Anchorage–Kona flies in winter (strong; supported by the check). The flight map explains 'Washington everywhere' (Seattle, Alaska Air Group's largest hub, flew 1.47M seats in 2025 to all four main airports) and the Kona lean of Alaskans (Anchorage–Kona winter nonstops since 2012; no Anchorage–Lihue seats). It does not explain Utah on Kauai (no SLC–Lihue nonstop in 2025 or the October 2026 schedule) or Puna lot buying (no Hilo mainland nonstop between January 2023 and August 2026). Seats and demand reinforce each other, and seats per resident alone do not rank states (Arizona has more than Utah but buys a third as much). Strength: strong for WA and AK island patterns, weak for the rest.
  • Lāʻie and BYU–Hawaiʻi ties explain where some Utah owners are (strong; supported by the check). Utah's most distinctive Hawaii tie is Laie on Oahu. Utah addresses hold about 47% of the mainland-addressed parcels there (55 of 118), against 2% island-wide. In absolute terms that is about 6% of all Laie parcels. Utah buyers on Oahu overall are about average for an out-of-state group. This link explains where some Utah owners on Oahu are, not why Utah ranks among buyer states, and it says nothing about Kauai. Strength: strong locally, weak statewide.
  • Visitor funnel: western states send far more visitors per resident (a correlation, not proof) (moderate; weakened by the check). Western states send far more visitors per resident than Texas or Florida (WA 8.9, OR 7.5, UT 6.5, CO 5.1 per 100 residents vs TX 1.1, FL 0.7), and their visitors repeat more often (6.2–8.4 average trips vs 4.2–4.5). Across 10 states, visitor rates track buyer rates closely (log r ≈ 0.95), but that mostly reflects the gap between the West and everyone else. Within the West, visitor rates do not predict which state buys more. A state's visitor island lean roughly predicts its buyer island lean (r ≈ 0.8 over 21 cells), with exceptions (Washington on Maui). Some of the repeat-visit signal probably comes from people who already own homes here. About 72% of Alaskan purchases are on Hawaii Island (Jan–Jun 2025), not almost all. Strength: moderate.
  • Winter escape: strong for Alaska only (moderate; weakened by the check). Winter escape is strong for Alaska (63% of trips in Nov–Mar, 10.75-day stays on Hawaii Island, and buying concentrated near Kona). For Oregon, Washington, Utah and Colorado the evidence is weak: Arizona, with a warm winter, has a higher winter share of trips than Colorado, so seasonal timing mostly reflects Hawaii's high season and school breaks. Strength: strong for Alaska, weak otherwise.
  • Price: Hawaiʻi Island is cheapest, which shapes where Alaskans and Oregonians buy, not whether they buy (moderate; weakened by the check). Price shapes how much these buyers spend, not which states they come from. Hawaii Island is the cheapest island, and Alaskans buy there in the mid-market (about $708k on average in 2024–25). Oregonians and Washingtonians, like Californians, also buy cheap Puna lots (about $215–272k). Home-equity gains do not explain the list: Florida, Arizona and Nevada gained as much or more than Utah, Washington and Colorado but rarely buy. Strength: moderate for price tier, weak for state selection.
  • Family and migration ties: real for Nevada, Washington, Oregon and Alaska (moderate; weakened by the check). Family and migration ties add pull for Nevada, Washington, Oregon and Alaska, where many former Hawaii households live (IRS 2011–23: Hawaii lost a net 6,667 households to Washington and 9,900 to Nevada). They do not explain Utah or Colorado well, and part of the two-way flow is military moves rather than family. Strength: moderate for NV/WA/AK, weak for UT/CO.
  • Colorado and Utah on Kauaʻi: clear in visitor data, small and unstable in buyer data (weak; weakened by the check). Colorado and Utah visitors really do favor Kauai (about 1.5–1.65 times the US average share, even after adjusting for multi-island trips), with or without a nonstop. Their buying on Kauai is small (3–24 sales a year) and unstable. Colorado's 2025 jump came largely from 12 sub-$500k Hanalei purchases in one half-year, and both states were back to an average share in Jan–Jun 2026. Kauai's resort-zone rental rules, more than buyer origin, explain why they buy in Poipu and Princeville. Strength: moderate for visitors, weak for buyers.

Why

Why buyers from Japan and Korea concentrate on Oʻahu, and why they jumped in 2026

Japan's ties to Hawaiʻi run through Honolulu. Every flight from Japan lands there, 98% of Japanese visitors spend time on Oʻahu, and owners with Japan mailing addresses already hold about 2,000 Oʻahu parcels, nearly all condos. The 2026 rise in buyers from Japan despite a weak yen is mostly one tower. The Park Ward Village closed 527 pre-sold units in Q2 2026, on contracts signed in 2021–22 when the yen was ¥112–123 to the dollar. Outside that building, purchases by buyers with Japan addresses fell to about 72 on Oʻahu, from 84 a year earlier. Purchases by buyers with Korea addresses jumped the same way, when Victoria Place (late 2024) and The Park on Keʻeaumoku (late 2025) closed.

  1. StrongTower closings: pre-sold contracts are recorded only when the building delivers
  2. StrongLinks only to Oʻahu: flights, repeat visits and an existing base of Japanese condo owners
  3. ModerateDevelopers market Honolulu towers in Tokyo
  4. ModerateThe weak yen is a drag on new contracts, not a cause of the 2026 rise
  5. WeakWealth and diversification out of the yen and won helped buyers close; they did not add new buying
  6. WeakHome-country rules: Korea's 2020 multi-home taxes came just before the Korean pre-sale wave
  7. WeakFlight capacity explains where they buy, not when
Reading the data

Counts of buyers with Japan or Korea addresses track tower delivery schedules more than the exchange rate: Oʻahu recorded only 32 Japan-address purchases in Q1 2026, before the tower closed. With the yen near ¥158, new contracts from Japan are likely to stay soft.

For local families

Buyers with Japan or Korea addresses made about 2.6% of Oʻahu purchases in 2025 (289 of 11,097). They bought mostly new Kakaʻako and Ala Moana tower units and Waikīkī resort condos, priced well above the Oʻahu condo median, so most local condo shoppers aren't bidding against them. Where they matter is specific buildings, where part-time occupancy runs high.

The full explanation, each driver as checked, and 31 sources

The checked answer

Japan leads foreign buying on Oahu because its ties to Hawaii run almost entirely through Honolulu. All scheduled seats from Japan land there (DBEDT, May 2026). 97.6% of the 749,596 Japanese visitors in 2025 spent time on Oahu, and 71% were repeat visitors. Owners with Japan mailing addresses already hold about 2,000 Oʻahu parcels, nearly all condo units in Waikiki and Ala Moana/Kakaako. Ward Village has also been sold in Tokyo through Mitsui Fudosan Realty. The H1 2026 'rise' is not new demand defying a weak yen. It is the recording of contracts signed in 2021-22, when the yen was about ¥112-123, at The Park Ward Village. Howard Hughes closed 527 units there in Q2 2026, the same quarter Oahu purchases by buyers from Japan jumped from 32 to 101. Outside that building, purchases by buyers with Japan addresses on Oʻahu ran about 72 in H1 2026 against 84 a year earlier. buying from Korea followed the same pattern twice. 31 of 2024's 40 purchases by buyers from Korea came in Q4 2024, when Victoria Place closed. 79 of 2025's 87 came in the second half, when The Park on Keeaumoku began closing. In quarters with no tower deliveries, Koreans bought only 2-6 Oahu homes per quarter. History shows the same thing. purchases by buyers from Japan on Oʻahu fell from 581 in 2018 (the year Ae'o delivered) to 319 in 2019, even though the yen was flat and Japanese arrivals rose. Currency, stock-market wealth and home-country rules affect whether contracts get signed, but the evidence for them is aggregate and circumstantial. The clearest well-timed factor on the Korean side is Seoul's 2020 tax increases on multi-home owners, which came just before the 2021-22 pre-sale wave. Matching tax-roll owners to quarterly purchases is approximate, and buyer-address counts are a floor. With no Ward Village tower due before 2028, recorded Japanese and purchases by buyers from Korea should fall back toward their non-delivery pace (an inference; other developers' deliveries were not checked). Confidence: high on the timing explanation, medium on the underlying motives.

Each driver, as checked

  • Tower closings: pre-sold contracts are recorded only when the building delivers (strong; supported by the check). Recorded Japanese and purchases by buyers from Korea on Oahu track when big pre-sold towers deliver, not when buyers decide. Oahu purchases by buyers from Japan jumped from 32 in Q1 2026 to 101 in Q2 2026, the quarter Howard Hughes closed 527 units at The Park Ward Village. Those contracts were signed mainly in July 2021-mid 2022, when the yen was about ¥112-123. Outside that tower, purchases by buyers with Japan addresses were roughly 72 in H1 2026 vs 84 in H1 2025. Korea shows the same pattern twice: 31 of 2024's 40 purchases by buyers from Korea came in Q4 2024 as Victoria Place closed, and 79 of 2025's 87 came in H2 2025 as The Park on Keeaumoku began closing. In quarters with no deliveries, Koreans bought 2-6 Oahu homes per quarter. Matching buildings to quarterly purchases is approximate, not a transaction-level match.
  • Links only to Oʻahu: flights, repeat visits and an existing base of Japanese condo owners (strong; supported by the check). Oahu and Honolulu condos dominate because Japan's links to Hawaii run only through Oahu. All scheduled Japan-Hawaii seats land at Honolulu (DBEDT, May 2026), 97.6% of 2025 Japanese visitors spent time on Oahu, 71% were repeat visitors, and owners with Japan addresses already hold about 2,000 Oahu parcels, almost all condo units in Waikiki and Ala Moana/Kakaako. This explains where buyers from Japan buy, not why the count moves from year to year. It explains little about buyers from Korea, two-thirds of whom are first-time visitors.
  • Developers market Honolulu towers in Tokyo (moderate; supported by the check). Ward Village has been sold in Japan through Mitsui Fudosan Realty and others. In 2019 Howard Hughes put buyers from Japan at 19% of Ward Village contracts. Marketing channels plausibly steer which buildings buyers from Japan choose, but they do not explain the national totals, and the channel effect cannot be separated from price and product.
  • The weak yen is a drag on new contracts, not a cause of the 2026 rise (moderate; supported by the check). The weak yen (¥158 in H1 2026 vs ¥109 in 2019) raises the yen cost of a Honolulu condo and is a plausible drag on new Japanese contracts. It cannot explain the 2026 jump, which was closings of dollar-priced contracts signed at ¥112-123. Japanese purchase value fell about 13% a year in real terms from 2016 to 2025 (DBEDT), but that decline also reflects Covid, fewer visitors, tower timing and a 2021 Japanese tax change.

Resort areas (Lahaina, Kihei, Princeville, Poipu, Kona, Waikoloa, Waikiki) run 29–54% investor loans; non-resort towns on every island (Kahului, Wailuku, Mililani, Ewa, Waipahu) run 3–12%. Resort amenities and past investor buying are tangled up with zoning, so this is an association, not proof that zoning alone causes it. The military answers the VA question but explains only a small part of the investor gap. About 43,700 active-duty members and 44,100 dependents live on Oahu, against fewer than 900 people combined on all other islands. VA's terms make it their default loan: no down payment, no mortgage insurance, no loan cap with full entitlement, looser debt limits and rates about half a point lower. Honolulu's VA share is normal for a U.S. military town: 24.7% of 2025 purchase applications, about the same as Anchorage (24.6%) and below Virginia Beach (37.5%) and Colorado Springs' El Paso County (35.4%). Taking VA loans out lifts Oahu's investor share only to 17.2%, which closes 2–3 of the 10–18 points. Three cautions matter. First, the 'investor' label shifted. Since 2019, lenders have recoded vacation-home loans from 'second home' to 'investment', and lenders that don't verify income grew from about 1% to 4–10% of purchase loans. The combined second-home-plus-investor share barely moved: 14–16% on Oahu and 30–40% on the neighbor islands. Second, Hawaii Island is a different story. Its investor-only share equaled Oahu's in 2019 (10.5% vs 10.3%). Much of its 2025 gap sits in Puna, where $250K–450K homes can pay for themselves as long-term rentals, and one bridge lender charging about 10.5% made 77 of the county's 405 investor loans. Third, HMDA leaves out cash buyers. On Maui, 57% of FY2025 home sales went to buyers not eligible for the homeowner exemption, against 34% of mortgaged buyers, so the real gap with Oahu is probably wider. Oahu's 90-day rental minimum, military housing allowances and conforming loan limits explain little of the difference between islands.

Each driver, as checked

  • Where vacation rentals operate (an association, not proof) (strong; supported by the check). Across 47 ZIP codes, the share of homes used as short-term rentals explains nearly two-thirds of the variation in investor share of mortgaged purchases. Once it is accounted for, being on Oahu makes no difference. Resort ZIPs run 29–54% investor (Lahaina, Kihei, Princeville, Koloa/Poipu, Kona, Waikoloa, Waikiki), while non-resort towns on every island run 3–12% (Kahului, Wailuku, Kalaheo, Mililani, Ewa, Waipahu). Exceptions are Puna and Hilo on Hawaii Island (19–48%) and Ala Moana/Ward on Oahu (29.5%), where investor buying is not tied to STRs. Because STR stock partly reflects past investor buying and resort amenities, this shows association with vacation-rental geography, not a clean zoning effect.
  • Oʻahu's military population (strong; supported by the check). VA loans are 27% of Oahu purchase loans because about 43,700 active-duty members and 44,100 dependents live on Oahu, against fewer than 900 people combined on all other islands. Honolulu's VA share (24.7% of 2025 purchase applications) is typical of U.S. military-host counties. It is in line with Anchorage (24.6%) and below Virginia Beach (37.5%) and El Paso County, Colorado (35.4%). These owner-occupant VA buyers dilute Oahu's investor share only modestly. Removing them lifts it from 12.7% to 17.2%, which closes 2–3 of the 10–18 point gap.
  • VA loan terms: the cheapest way to buy for those eligible (strong; supported by the check). For eligible buyers, VA is the cheapest way to buy on Oahu. Of VA loans that report a loan-to-value ratio, 61% financed 100% or more of the value. The median VA rate was 5.875% vs 6.375% for conventional owner-occupant loans. 47% of VA borrowers had debt-to-income of 50% or more, vs 1% of conventional ones. VA also finances above the conforming limit with no down payment: 172 of 436 Oahu loans above $1,209,750 in 2025 were VA. VA's share of owner-occupant purchases holds at 31–35% from under $500K up to $1.5M.
  • How lenders label loans: vacation homes recoded from 'second home' to 'investment' (moderate; supported by the check). Part of the 23–31% investor figure is a labeling and lending effect. Since 2019, lenders moved vacation-home loans from 'second home' to 'investment', so the combined non-owner share barely changed (Oahu 14–16%; neighbor islands 30–40%). Meanwhile, lenders that don't verify income grew from about 1% to 4–10% of all purchase loans. Without those loans, 2025 investor shares are Kauai 21%, Maui 19%, Hawaii Island 13% and Oahu 9%. On Hawaii Island, one bridge lender charging about 10.5% made 77 of 405 investor loans, mostly in Puna.
  • Military rotations and housing allowances keep VA buyers coming (weak; weakened by the check). Steady military turnover keeps feeding VA buyers. 22% of people who moved to Hawaii from another state in the past year were active duty (ACS 2024). 2026 housing allowances for mid-grade families ($3,663–$4,428) roughly match principal and interest on a median Oahu VA loan, before taxes, insurance and HOA dues. Because the allowance is set at local rents, buying is not clearly cheaper than renting each month. The appeal is zero-down equity. Allowance levels do not explain the difference between islands.
  • Long-term rents rarely cover a financed payment, except in Puna (weak; supported by the check). Long-term rental demand does not explain Oahu's low investor share. At Oahu prices, a 70%-financed condo or house does not cover its payment from rent, and investor shares in Oahu suburbs are 3–6%. The exception is Puna on Hawaii Island. There, $250K–450K homes rent for $1,350–1,750, gross yields reach 5–8%, and investor loans are 17–25% of purchases despite few legal vacation rentals.
  • Oʻahu's 90-day rental minimum is not the reason (weak; supported by the check). Oahu's 90-day minimum is not why Oahu's investor share is low. The share was already 10.3% in 2019, and the investor hot spot, Waikiki, is resort-zoned and unaffected. Outside lenders that don't verify income, Oahu's investor share actually slipped from 9.3% to 8.8% between 2019 and 2025.
  • Loan limits are the same on every island (weak; supported by the check). Conforming loan limits were the same on every island in 2025 ($1,209,750), so they do not explain the investor gap. They matter on Oahu only because VA buyers with full entitlement can borrow above the limit with no down payment. 172 of the 436 Oahu purchase loans above the limit in 2025 were VA.

affordability:
Why

Why a home now takes so much more of a local paycheck

Two shocks hit in sequence. First, prices jumped in 2020–22, mostly while rates were near 3% (2020–21) and listings had nearly vanished. Then mortgage rates averaged 6.6% in 2025, up from 3.9% in 2019, which raised the payment on every borrowed dollar by 35%, and prices did not fall back. On Oʻahu the two pushed about equally: each added 14–24 points, depending on which is counted first. On Maui and Kauaʻi prices pushed harder, adding 30–41 points against 13–25 for rates. Rising incomes took back part of it. Hawaiʻi's chronic limits explain why the starting point was already about 40%: slow permits, little urban land and high building costs.

  2. StrongMortgage rates: about as big as prices on Oʻahu, and nearly all of the rise since 2021
  3. ModerateIncome growth took some of it back
  4. ModerateChronic supply limits: why it started high and didn't fall
  5. ModerateVacation rentals and second homes raise Maui and Kauaʻi price levels
  6. ModerateCondo insurance and dues are not in the headline figure, and add 6–10 points of income for an Oʻahu condo buyer
  7. WeakConstruction costs: a modest, indirect push
  8. WeakOutside buyers: behind neighbor-island price levels and the 2021–22 spike
Reading the data

Each point of mortgage rate moves the payment about 10–11%. At the October 8 rate of 7.40%, the report's formula, using 2026-to-date median prices and 2024 incomes, gives about 75% of income on Oʻahu, 82% on Maui and 89% on Kauaʻi. Condo insurance, reserves and special assessments now affect whether a condo purchase can be financed.

For local families

The headline figure compares one median house with one median household. It leaves out taxes, insurance and condo dues, so treat it as a gauge, not a budget. Rates matter most now: a one-point drop is worth roughly a 10% price cut. But prices also rose faster than pay in 2020–22, so lower rates alone won't bring back 2019 conditions. The lasting fix is more housing, which depends on permit speed and zoning.

The full explanation, each driver as checked, and 24 sources

The checked answer

The report's own formula checks out: principal and interest on a 30-year loan with 20% down on the county's median single-family price, divided by median household income. On it, Oahu went from 41% of income in 2019 to 66% in 2025, Maui from 42% to 78%, Kauai from 37% to 76%, and Hawaii Island from 26% to 46%. Two things drove the rise, in sequence. First, prices jumped in 2020–22, while rates were near 3%, listings had nearly vanished and wealthier mainland buyers and in-movers were active. Higher prices account for about 19 of Oahu's 25-point rise and 32–33 points on Maui and Kauai. Second, mortgage rates jumped in 2022–23; they averaged 6.6% in 2025 against 3.9% in 2019, which raised the payment on every borrowed dollar by 35%. That added about 16–18 points, and prices did not fall back. Since 2021, rates explain nearly all of Oahu's increase. Income growth of about 20% (12.5% on Hawaii Island) took back roughly 10–14 points on the three most expensive islands. Hawaii's long-standing limits explain why the starting point was already 40% of income and why prices held when rates rose: slow permits (a median of 394 days for an Oahu single-family permit), very little urban land and high building costs. So does a rising share of all-cash buyers, roughly 31% to 42% of recorded sales by a rough proxy. Supply did tighten somewhat after 2019. The housing stock grew about 0.5% a year, down from 0.8%, while the number of households grew faster than the number of homes. Outside buyers mainly explain the high neighbor-island prices and the 2021–22 spike. Statewide their share of sales is back near 2019 levels, but on Oahu it rose from 13% to 17%, and the out-of-state share of purchase dollars rose statewide. Vacation rentals raise price levels on Kauai and Maui, where they are 15–20% of homes. New limits on them are now pulling Maui condo prices down (11% below 2023). Condo dues and insurance are not in the 66–78% figure. Dues alone add about 6–10 points of income for an Oahu condo buyer, and insurance premiums rose 13.4% statewide in 2024. How much of that cost is new since 2023 has not been measured. The headline also holds 2025 income at its 2024 level, which overstates the burden by 2–3 points, and leaves out taxes, insurance and dues, which understates it. At the October 8, 2026 rate of 7.40%, the same formula gives about 75% on Oahu, 82% on Maui and 89% on Kauai.

Each driver, as checked

  • The 2020–22 price run-up: the largest piece (strong; supported by the check). Higher prices were the largest piece from 2019 to 2025: about 19 of Oahu's 25-point rise and 32–33 of the 36–39-point rises on Maui and Kauai. Almost all of it came in 2020–22, while rates were near 3% and listings fell below two months of supply. On Oahu the rise (+44–46%) was in line with the rest of the country or below it. Maui's and Kauai's single-family medians (+71% and +83%) rose faster than the typical state's (+61% on FHFA), but they rest on thin sales.
  • Mortgage rates: about as big as prices on Oʻahu, and nearly all of the rise since 2021 (strong; supported by the check). Mortgage rates rose from 3.9% (2019 average) to 6.6% (2025), which raises the payment on every borrowed dollar by 35%. That added 16–18 points on Oahu, Maui and Kauai, and almost all of the increase since 2021. Rates peaked at 7.79% in October 2023, first dipped below 6% on Feb 26, 2026, and were 7.40% on Oct 8, 2026. At today's rate the same formula gives about 75% on Oahu, 82% on Maui and 89% on Kauai.
  • Income growth took some of it back (moderate; supported by the check). Median household income rose about 20% on Oahu and Kauai (2019–2024) and 12.5% on Hawaii Island. That took back about 10 points on Oahu and Kauai and 4 on Hawaii Island. Maui's apparent +25% rests on a volatile survey estimate. Financed purchases fell 28% statewide and 56% on Maui, and the median borrower's income rose about 40%. Lower-income households were priced out, so the people still buying are a narrower, higher-income group.
  • Chronic supply limits: why it started high and didn't fall (moderate; weakened by the check). Hawaii's supply limits are mainly a long-standing condition rather than a 2019–25 shock. They explain why a median house already took 40% of income in 2019, and they helped keep prices from falling when rates rose. Supply growth did slow after 2019, however: the housing stock grew 0.5% a year against 0.8% a year in 2010–19, and permits dipped from about 4,200 to about 3,700 a year. Meanwhile the number of households grew faster than the number of homes, as average household size shrank.
  • Vacation rentals and second homes raise Maui and Kauaʻi price levels (moderate; supported by the check). Vacation rentals and second homes take a large share of the housing on Kauai (about 20% of units) and Maui (15%), which helps explain those islands' high price levels. Listings have crept up since the pandemic. Restrictions are now pushing the other way: Maui condo prices in 2025 were 11% below 2023 (16% for apartment-zoned STR buildings), and UHERO estimates a full Bill 9 phase-out could cut those condo prices 20–40%.
  • Condo insurance and dues are not in the headline figure, and add 6–10 points of income for an Oʻahu condo buyer (moderate; weakened by the check). Condo ownership costs more than the mortgage alone. HOA/AOAO dues of $526 (Honolulu median among payers) to $882 (median Oahu listing) add about 6–10 points of income on top of a 30% condo payment. Insurance premiums rose 13.4% statewide in 2024, with far larger jumps for some older towers, so part of today's dues is new. How much of the increase dates from 2023–26 has not been measured. Higher carrying costs probably help explain why Oahu condo prices have been flat since 2022, alongside higher rates and the 90-day rental minimum.
  • Construction costs: a modest, indirect push (weak; weakened by the check). Honolulu building costs rose about 23% from 2019 to 2024 (construction cost index, preliminary), slightly faster than Oahu median income (+20%). That discourages new building and keeps a floor under prices, but it is a modest and indirect contributor to the 2019–25 jump in payments. No official Hawaii estimate of the Jones Act or union-wage premium was found.
  • Outside buyers: behind neighbor-island price levels and the 2021–22 spike (weak; weakened by the check). Outside money mainly explains why neighbor-island prices are so high and why prices spiked in 2021–22. On Maui, purchases by non-owner-occupants and the incomes of in-movers peaked in 2021–22 and then fell back. By count, the statewide out-of-state share is back near 2019 (22%). On Oahu it rose from 13% to 17%, mostly in condos (single-family 8.6% in 2025), and out-of-state buyers pay much more per purchase on Maui, Kauai and the Big Island. It is a secondary driver of the 2022–25 squeeze, not a non-factor.

Why

Why departing households go where they go

Departing households leave mainly because of housing costs. They land where housing is cheaper and jobs have grown, the same pull that draws movers from every state. In August 2026 a typical Honolulu asking rent (Zillow Observed Rent Index) was about $1,300 a month above Las Vegas or Phoenix. Military orders are a separate channel, and taxes matter little.

  3. StrongMilitary orders: about 9% of Oʻahu's leavers go to base-dominated counties, about 18% counting Tacoma, San Antonio and El Paso
  4. StrongJobs: leavers follow the same job growth as other Americans
  5. WeakFamily and community networks: real for Las Vegas and Utah County
  6. WeakState income tax: about $1,600–3,400 a year, small next to housing costs
Reading the data

Las Vegas is the only strongly one-way corridor. Base-town flows (San Antonio, El Paso, Colorado Springs, Tacoma, San Diego) follow military orders. Flows to Denver and Salt Lake City are smaller (about 180–360 households a year) and run both ways. The housing payment gap, not taxes, is the larger cost difference.

For local families

The flow to Las Vegas fell 38% from its 2006–07 peak to 2009–10 (IRS years), as Nevada's economy collapsed: the cheapest destinations can have volatile job markets. Coming back is hard once Hawaiʻi prices move on. If you might return, weigh renting out your home instead of selling it. You would lose the homeowner exemption, and renting it out for more than three years would also cost you the federal capital-gains exclusion on a later sale, so get tax advice first.

The full explanation, each driver as checked, and 23 sources

The checked answer

Hawaii's departing households leave mainly because housing costs too much, and they land where housing is cheaper and jobs have grown. That mostly follows the same pull that draws movers from every state. Las Vegas is the one place Hawaii residents favor far more than other Americans do. The push is cost. In August 2026 a typical Honolulu asking rent ran about $3,020 a month, roughly $1,300 more than in Las Vegas or Phoenix. For a single-family buyer the payment gap is about $3,700 a month. O'ahu households that moved to another state reported less income than those who stayed ($70k vs $90k average AGI, 2022–23). From 2011–14 to 2019–23, Hawaii's moves to Colorado, Washington, Arizona, Oregon and Idaho grew no faster than all U.S. moves into those states. Over the same period Hawaii's moves to Nevada grew 54%, against 19% nationally. Las Vegas is also the only strongly one-way corridor: about 1,650 households a year leave for it, roughly 2.4 for every one that comes back. That fits a 'ninth island' community built since Boyd Gaming began marketing to Hawaii in the 1970s, and those who go have lower incomes, which fits a cost-driven move. The flow still depends on jobs there: it fell 38% when Nevada's economy collapsed in 2008–10. Military orders are a separate channel. Counties dominated by bases take about 9% of O'ahu's leavers, up to about 18% if Tacoma, San Antonio and El Paso are counted, and these moves explain roughly half of the departures to Colorado (Colorado Springs) and Texas. State income tax matters little, about $1,600–3,400 a year at typical leaver incomes, and flows to no-tax states grew no faster than flows to taxed ones. Calling the interior West the 'fastest-growing exit' holds only against a mid-2000s base. Since 2011, Las Vegas (+60%) and Phoenix (+36%) grew faster than Salt Lake City (+35%) and Denver (+30%). Only Utah, mainly Provo, shows a Hawaii-specific lift. Those corridors are small, about 180–360 households a year, and Salt Lake City departures have fallen since 2020–21. The IRS data stop in early 2023, so later events are not reflected. For families, the cheapest destinations, Las Vegas above all, also have the most volatile job markets.

Each driver, as checked

  • The housing-cost gap (strong; supported by the check). High housing costs are the main reason households leave, and every top destination is much cheaper. At August 2026 asking rents, a Honolulu renter pays about $1,300 a month more than in Las Vegas or Phoenix (about $15,000 a year). For a single-family buyer the payment gap is about $3,700 a month. The gap does not explain which corridors grew or when. Las Vegas departures bottomed in 2009–12, when its homes were cheapest relative to Hawaii, and peaked after 2019, when its prices were rising faster than Honolulu's.
  • Las Vegas, the 'ninth island': community, decades of casino marketing and frequent flights (strong; supported by the check). Las Vegas is the one destination Hawaii residents favor far more than other Americans do. From 2011–14 to 2019–23, Hawaii's moves to Nevada grew 54% while all U.S. moves into Nevada grew 19%, and about 2.4 households leave for Las Vegas for each one that comes back. Its lower costs fit the lower incomes of those who go (about $64k average AGI). The pull is reinforced by a Hawaii community dating to Boyd Gaming's 1970s marketing and by heavy visitor traffic. The flow still depends on Las Vegas jobs: it fell 38% when Nevada's job market collapsed in 2008–10.
  • Military orders: about 9% of Oʻahu's leavers go to base-dominated counties, about 18% counting Tacoma, San Antonio and El Paso (strong; supported by the check). Military orders are a separate channel that people do not choose. Counties dominated by bases take about 9% of O'ahu's departing households, rising to about 18% if mixed civilian-military metros such as Tacoma, San Antonio and El Paso are included, and more if San Diego is counted. Military moves make up about half of departures to Colorado (Colorado Springs) and to Texas (San Antonio, Killeen, El Paso), which inflates the apparent growth of those 'exits'. The neighbor islands send almost none.
  • Jobs: leavers follow the same job growth as other Americans (strong; supported by the check). Destinations that added jobs fastest also drew the fastest-growing share of Hawaii's leavers, but that is the national migration pattern, not something special about Hawaii. Outside Nevada, and to a lesser degree Utah, Hawaii's flows grew no faster than everyone else's moves into those states. On the Hawaii side, UHERO finds high prices and persistent local constraints drive departures from Honolulu more than low incomes, although income is now adding to the pressure.
  • Family and community networks: real for Las Vegas and Utah County (weak; weakened by the check). Community ties clearly help explain Las Vegas and probably the Utah County (Provo) corridor, where Hawaii's moves grew faster than the national flow. There is no evidence that networks drive moves to Denver or Boise: Hawaii's flows there grew no faster than everyone else's, and the growth of communities with Hawaiʻi roots by state does not line up with where Hawaii's leavers went.
  • State income tax: about $1,600–3,400 a year, small next to housing costs (weak; supported by the check). State income tax is a minor factor. At a typical leaver's income it is worth about $1,600–3,400 a year, against a housing-cost gap of about $15,000 a year in rent (more for owners). Hawaii's flows to no-tax states grew no faster than flows to states with income taxes, and Hawaii's 2026 standard-deduction increase narrows the gap further.

The checked answer

Hawaii's 2026 'turn toward buyers' is real but narrower and later than the headline numbers suggest, and most of the Kauai-versus-Oahu sales gap comes from how sales are counted. Recorded deeds include developer closings that never go through the MLS. Oahu's +9% recorded gain in the first half came from The Park Ward Village tower, which closed 527 pre-sold units in Q2 2026. Howard Hughes reported zero Ward Village closings a year earlier. Without the tower, Oahu recorded sales fell about 2%, and MLS resales were flat. Kauai's −34% is measured against Q2 2025, when Lihue recorded about 80 unusually cheap condo transfers (median about $63,000) that no source explains. Adjusted for those, Kauai's drop is about 18–21%, close to its MLS resale decline of 14–19% depending on the source. That decline is real, but it is mostly condos (−26%), and it came in the first quarter, when mortgage rates were at their 2026 low. Kauai house sales have been flat since April. The cause of Kauai's condo weakness is not clear from the data. Mortgage rates explain the late-2026 turn instead. The 30-year rate rose from a 6.05% February average to 7.40% on Oct 8, which raises the payment on the same loan 14.9%. Since then, pending sales have fallen on Oahu, Kauai and the Big Island, and September closings dropped sharply on Kauai and the Big Island. Most of the inventory and price-cut figures in the question are September snapshots. Averaged over 2026, listings are flat on Oahu and Kauai and up about 10% on Maui and the Big Island. Oahu houses remain a seller's market, with about 3 months of supply, 17 days on market and 100% of asking. House listings are 27% below 2019, and local and military buyers keep buying. Condos are the oversupplied segment on Oahu (listings 34% above 2019) and Maui (70% above). Rising HOA dues and insurance costs fit that pattern, but they have not been measured directly. Maui has been a buyer's market since 2024, after the fire and the first vacation-rental phase-out proposal, and is now clearing: condo sales are up 21% at about 7% lower prices. Bill 9's long-run effect is uncertain because the June 2026 hotel-zoning law and lawsuits may exempt thousands of units. Tourism softness and buyers from Canada explain little. The jump in buyers from Japan coincides with the Ward Village closings and likely reflects old presales, not new demand. For local families: Oahu house buyers get little relief from rising rates. Condo and neighbor-island buyers have leverage, but HOA fees, insurance deductibles and special assessments can cancel out a price discount. Confidence: high on the counting explanation, medium on the causes behind it.

Each driver, as checked

  • Recorded deeds vs MLS resales: one-time closings distort the headline (strong; supported by the check). Recorded deed counts and MLS resale counts measure different things. Oahu's +9.1% recorded gain in H1 2026 includes 527 pre-sold units at The Park Ward Village that closed in Q2 2026. Howard Hughes reported zero Ward Village closings in Q2 2025. Without them, Oahu recorded sales fell about 2%, and MLS resales were flat (+0.1%: houses +3.9%, condos −2.3%). Kauai's −33.5% is measured against Q2 2025, when Lihue recorded about 80 extra low-priced condo transfers of an undocumented type. Adjusted for those, Kauai recorded sales fell about 18–21%, in line with an MLS resale decline of 14–19% depending on the source.
  • Two markets: scarce Oʻahu houses, oversupplied condos (strong; supported by the check). Oahu and Maui have split by property type. Oahu house listings are 27% below August 2019 (794 vs 1,086), houses have about 3.2 months of supply, and they sell in a median 17 days at 100% of asking. Oahu condo listings are 34% above 2019 (about 6.9 months of supply), and Maui condo listings are 70% above, while Maui house listings are flat. Higher HOA dues, master-policy insurance and deductibles, and on Maui the vacation-rental phase-out, plausibly weigh on condos, but the data does not separate their effects. Low house turnover is consistent with rate lock-in (a national FHFA estimate) and steady local and military demand (VA loans were 27% of Honolulu purchase loans in 2025).
  • Mortgage rates drive the late-2026 cooling (moderate; supported by the check). Mortgage rates explain the timing of the late-2026 turn, not the first-half sales numbers. Rates averaged 6.27% in H1 2026 against 6.80% in H1 2025, and Kauai's sharpest drop (Q1 2026) came at the year's low. Since February (6.05% average) rates have risen to 7.40% (week of Oct 8), raising the payment on the same loan 14.9%. The rise came from Treasury yields, not a wider mortgage spread. Pending sales then fell on Oahu, Kauai and the Big Island, and September closings dropped sharply on Kauai and the Big Island. Maui pending sales and Oahu house closings kept rising, so rates set the timing but local conditions decide how hard each market is hit.
  • Data quirks: Realtor.com quality flags and different months-of-supply definitions (moderate; supported by the check). Several headline numbers depend on the data source. Maui's Realtor.com data has been quality-flagged every month since December 2025, and Maui's months of supply is 9.6 by the report's method but 11.0 by the Maui board's (houses 7.8, condos 12.1). Kauai's 4.8% September price-cut share is an artifact (24 reduced of 385, against 15.2% in August). Realtor.com's 2019 Hawaii series is unreliable, so use board inventory for comparisons with 2019. Recorded-deed and MLS counts differ: Maui recorded 643 sales in H1 2026 against 759 MLS sales, and new-tower closings inflate or deflate Oahu's recorded year-over-year changes.
  • Fewer buyers on Kauaʻi and Hawaiʻi Island, concentrated in Kauaʻi condos (weak; weakened by the check). On Kauai, sales fell because fewer buyers came, but the drop is concentrated in condos (MLS −26% Jan–Aug) and in Q1 2026 (−31%), when mortgage rates were at their lowest of the year. Kauai house sales have been flat since April, and sellers are also listing less (new listings −9.5% Jan–Sep). On the Big Island, MLS sales were nearly flat through August (−3%). The turn is recent: listings rose through the summer (+25% YoY in September per Realtor.com) and closings fell in September. Mainland buyers declined on both islands (Kauai −31%, Big Island −16% in H1 recorded sales).
  • Maui has been a buyer's market since 2024 and is now clearing (weak; weakened by the check). Maui's condo glut began in 2024, after the Lahaina fire and when the vacation-rental phase-out was first proposed, and Bill 9 (signed Dec 15, 2025; deadlines 2029/2031) sustains it. In 2026, Maui is clearing rather than newly turning. Condo months of supply is 12.1, down from 15.2. Condo closings are up 21% at a median 6.8% lower, and condo pending sales are up 22% YTD. The June 2026 hotel-zoning law (Bill 88) and pending lawsuits may let thousands of units keep renting to visitors, which makes Bill 9's final effect uncertain.
  • Tourism explains little (weak; supported by the check). Tourism explains little. In H1 2026, Kauai visitor arrivals were up 2.8% and spending was down 0.8%, so tourism did not cause Kauai's first-half sales drop. Softness came later: August arrivals fell about 5.6% statewide (Hurricane Lala Aug 14–16, Tropical Storm Moke Aug 22–24), Kauai international arrivals were −13.7% Jan–Aug, and WestJet is dropping Kauai's only Canada nonstop from December 2026 (reported). That weighs on the outlook more than on 2026 sales.
  • Buyers from Canada and Japan are too few to move island markets (weak; supported by the check). Foreign buyers are too few to move island markets (about 3% of H1 2026 recorded sales). Canada's drop (49 → 26) was entirely on Oahu. purchases by buyers from Canada on the other islands held at 18, so Canada explains none of the neighbor-island slowdown. Japan's rise (91 → 138) came mostly in Q2 2026 in Honolulu, the quarter The Park Ward Village closed, so it likely reflects old presales rather than new demand.

Kahuku town, Lāʻie and Hauʻula houses, and the wider Kahala–Kaimukī ZIP are 85–98% locally owned. The exception is the $10M+ tier: most Oʻahu homes at that level have no homeowner exemption and are often held by entities.

For local families

Off-island competition is sharpest for older condos in Waikīkī and Punaluʻu, which are often a family's first purchase; in Hauʻula, mainland buyers in 2023–25 paid a median of about $439K (28 sales). The full explanation, each driver as checked, and 27 sources

The checked answer

On O'ahu, off-island ownership is concentrated in particular buildings and plats, not whole neighborhoods. The ZIP rankings mostly reflect how big those pockets are relative to their ZIP. The clearest pockets are units run as visitor lodging. Hotel-and-resort-class condos are about 52% owned off-island across Oahu, and the Ala Moana Hotel condo is 43%. The resort-zoned enclaves follow the same pattern: Kuilima/Turtle Bay is about half off-island, against 2–5% in Kahuku town; Ko Olina is 38–42% and Mākaha 27–39%. Kahuku ranks second, behind Waikīkī, because Turtle Bay makes up half of a tiny ZIP. Ko Olina is nearly as off-island-owned but is hidden inside the large Kapolei–Makakilo ZIP. Hau'ula's figure comes from Punalu'u condos (44% off-island) plus Utah-linked owners. Lā'ie's comes mostly from Utah-linked owners, including institutional addresses, and the North Shore's from scattered high-end and condo second homes. Ala Moana–Kaka'ako ties the North Shore at 17% but is missing from the question, and it shows a second route: mainland and buyers from Japan purchase new tower units as second homes, with almost no vacation renting. Across ZIPs, off-island ownership rises with the share of homes listed for vacation rental (r ≈ 0.9) and not with price. That listing count includes illegal units and partly restates absentee ownership, so it shows the two occur together rather than proving that rental rules drive the buying.

Neighbor-island luxury is concentrated where the luxury product was built: master-planned resort and private-club communities, from Ka'anapali (1962) to Hualālai (1996) and the newer North Kona clubs. By a brokerage's map counts, South Kohala and North Kona took about 86% of Hawai'i Island's 2025 $3M+ house sales, and West and South Maui took 82% of Maui's; on Maui the Kapalua, Kāʻanapali and Wailea–Mākena resorts alone took 40 of 71. Dry leeward weather helped site those resorts but is not required; Kaua'i's rainy North Shore is also a luxury hub. The argument that Hawai'i is cheap next to mainland trophy towns explains why buyers come to Hawai'i, not where they buy. Kahala is the exception: an older residential enclave of large lots near Wai'alae Country Club with no short-stay product, where buyers below roughly $5–10M are mostly local. Across Oahu, homes at $10M and up are mostly not owner-occupied and are often held by entities.

The ban on unsolicited offers in ZIPs 96761, 96767 and 96790 remains in the Thirty-Second Wildfire Proclamation (signed Aug 24, 2026) through Oct 23, 2026 unless extended.

For local families: most homes in these ZIPs remain 85–98% locally owned, including Kahuku town, Lā'ie and Hau'ula houses, and the wider Kahala–Kaimukī ZIP. Direct competition is sharpest for older condos in Waikīkī and Punalu'u; in Hau'ula, mainland buyers paid a median of about $439K.

Confidence: medium on the Oahu pattern, where plat-level data is strong but cause and effect is uncertain. Medium-low on why luxury sits where it does, since that rests on company-reported, small counts.

Policy details (Honolulu Ordinance 25-44, Act 17 and Maui's September 2026 rezoning vote) are as reported.

Each driver, as checked

  • Condos and condotels: lock-and-leave units (strong; supported by the check). Off-island owners mostly hold condos: about 13% of Oahu condo units against 5% of houses, and about half of hotel-and-resort-class units. Small managed units suit part-time use or rental. This holds where units can legally rent to visitors (Waikiki hotel-condos, Kuilima, Ko Olina) and also where they mostly cannot (Kaka'ako towers).
  • Master-planned resort and club communities (strong; supported by the check). On Hawai'i Island and Maui, $3M+ house sales cluster in a few master-planned resort and private-club communities. These were built in waves from 1962 (Ka'anapali) through the 1990s and later (Hualalai 1996, then the Kuki'o and Kohanaiki clubs). A brokerage's map counts put about 86% of Hawai'i Island's 2025 $3M+ house sales in South Kohala and North Kona and 82% of Maui's in West and South Maui; on Maui the Kapalua, Kāʻanapali and Wailea–Mākena resorts alone took 40 of 71. The enclaves offer new construction, golf and club amenities, and beach frontage that older towns lack. Most purchases there show no reported purchase mortgage.
  • Where visitor rentals are legal or grandfathered (an association, not proof) (moderate; weakened by the check). Off-island owners cluster in buildings and plats run as visitor lodging. These are hotel-and-resort-class condos in Waikiki and Ala Moana, and the resort-zoned enclaves at Kuilima/Turtle Bay, Ko Olina and Makaha. In those plats 27-53% of units are owned off-island, against 2-5% in neighboring town plats. Across ZIPs, off-island ownership tracks the share of homes listed on vacation-rental platforms (r about 0.9). That measure counts legal and illegal listings alike and partly restates absentee ownership, so it shows the two occur together, not that rental rules cause the buying.
  • Kahala: older wealth, large lots, no short-stay rentals (weak; weakened by the check). Kahala is Honolulu's established luxury enclave: large oceanfront and golf-course lots near Wai'alae Country Club, in a residential zone where short-stay rentals are barred. Oahu luxury homes below roughly $5-10M mostly go to Hawai'i residents. The trophy tier is different: most $10M+ Oahu homes carry no homeowner exemption and are often held by entities, so Kahala's top estates are not reliably 'local'.
  • Dry, sunny coasts helped site the resorts but aren't required (weak; weakened by the check). The Hawai'i Island and Maui resort coasts are among the driest places in the state (Kawaihae about 9 in/yr, Ka'anapali about 23, Kapalua about 28). That made them good sites for resorts and golf. Kaua'i's rainy North Shore (Princeville about 75 in/yr) shows that scenery, beaches and a resort or club community can sustain luxury demand without a dry climate.
  • West Coast wealth explains why buyers come, not where they buy (weak; weakened by the check). Off-island buyers come mainly from the Bay Area, Los Angeles and Seattle, the same metros that send the most visitors. On the neighbor islands they pay about 2-2.5 times what local buyers pay. Whether Hawai'i looks cheap against mainland resort towns depends on the comparison. This factor explains who buys in Hawai'i, not which neighborhoods they choose.
  • Koʻolauloa community ties: Utah-linked owners in Lāʻie and Hauʻula (weak; supported by the check). In Ko'olauloa (La'ie, Hau'ula, Kahuku), a notable minority of off-island owners mail to Utah: 45% in La'ie and 14-18% in Hau'ula and Kahuku. Some are institutions and some are likely families tied to BYU–Hawaiʻi. Part of the area's off-island ownership therefore reflects community ties, not resort demand.
